title: Amazon's Free Shipping: Who Really Pays?
summary: Amazon spent $102.7 billion on shipping in 2025, more than twice what all its subscriptions brought in. Here's where the rest of the money comes from: $172.2 billion in seller fees, $68.6 billion in ads, and the prices you see.

hooks.hook: Last year Amazon spent $102.7 billion just shipping packages, and for millions of shoppers the shipping was free.
Who actually pays for Amazon's free shipping? Not your Prime fee.
Free shipping is one of the most expensive things Amazon sells.

sources: Amazon.com 2025 Form 10-K (MD&A): "Shipping costs were $95.8 billion and $102.7 billion in 2024 and 2025"; service sales "primarily represent third-party seller fees, which includes commissions and any related fulfillment and shipping fees"; Item 1: Amazon Prime, "a membership program that includes fast, free shipping on tens of millions of items": https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1018724/000101872426000004/amzn-20251231.htm

Amazon.com 2025 Form 10-K, Segment Information - Disaggregation of Revenue: 2025 third-party seller services $172,162M, advertising services $68,635M, subscription services $49,619M, total net sales $716,924M: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1018724/000101872426000004/R88.htm

Amazon press release, Feb 2, 2005 (SEC Exhibit 99.1): Amazon Prime introduced, $79 a year for unlimited express two-day shipping: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1018724/000119312505017451/dex991.htm

FTC press release, Sept 26, 2023 (FTC v. Amazon): "Combined, all of these fees force many sellers to pay close to 50% of their total revenues to Amazon"; advertising fees "have become virtually necessary for sellers to do business"; Prime eligibility "a virtual necessity", conditioned "on sellers using Amazon's costly fulfillment service"; "Anti-discounting measures that punish sellers ... offering prices lower than Amazon": https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2023/09/ftc-sues-amazon-illegally-maintaining-monopoly-power

FTC and plaintiff states v. Amazon.com, No. 2:23-cv-01495 (W.D. Wash.), case pending (claims are allegations): https://www.naag.org/multistate-case/ftc-and-plaintiff-states-v-amazon-com-inc-no-223-cv-01495-w-d-wash-sept-26-2023/

Amazon to pay $2.5 billion to settle FTC allegations it duped customers into enrolling in Prime (AP via PBS, Sept 25, 2025): https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/amazon-to-pay-2-5-billion-to-settle-ftc-allegations-it-duped-customers-into-enrolling-in-prime

Our math: $49.6B subscriptions / $102.7B shipping = 48%; $172.2B seller fees - $102.7B shipping = $69.5B. Subscription services also include digital subscriptions, so Prime fees alone are less than $49.6B. Ads are bought by sellers, vendors and other businesses; "mostly businesses" is our wording.

scenes.narration: Last year, Amazon spent {$102.7 billion|one hundred two point seven billion dollars} just shipping packages. And for millions of shoppers, the shipping was free.
So who actually paid that bill? Not your Prime fee. Not really. The money comes from somewhere most shoppers never look.
By the end, you'll know exactly who pays for the box on your doorstep. And it might be you.
Part one. The seventy-nine dollar promise.
In {2005,|two thousand five,} Amazon launched Prime. {$79|Seventy-nine dollars} a year, for unlimited two-day shipping.
The idea was simple. Pay once, and every order after that feels free.

Now jump to {2025.|twenty twenty-five.} Shipping cost Amazon {$102.7 billion.|one hundred two point seven billion.} All its subscriptions together, Prime fees included, brought in {$49.6 billion.|forty-nine point six billion.}
Even if every one of those dollars were a Prime fee, it would cover less than half the shipping bill.
If you like seeing the receipts behind everyday prices, subscribe. New ones every other day.
Part two. The sellers' bill.
Here's what most shoppers miss. A lot of what you buy on Amazon isn't sold by Amazon. It's sold by other businesses, renting space in Amazon's store.

In {2025,|twenty twenty-five,} those sellers paid Amazon {$172.2 billion|one hundred seventy-two point two billion dollars} in fees. Commissions on every sale, plus fees for storing and shipping their goods.
That's more than the entire shipping bill, by about seventy billion dollars.
And then there are ads. Another {$68.6 billion,|sixty-eight point six billion,} mostly from businesses paying to show up when you search.
In {2023,|twenty twenty-three,} the US government sued Amazon, and put a number on it. Combined, all of these fees force many sellers to pay close to fifty percent of their total revenues to Amazon.

data.quote: ...force many sellers to pay *close to 50%* of their total revenues to Amazon.
data.note: lawsuit, Sept 2023; Amazon is fighting it

scenes.narration: The government also says the Prime badge is a virtual necessity for sellers, and that getting it is tied to using Amazon's own delivery service.
Part three. Who really pays.
So follow the money. You pay for Prime. Sellers pay commissions, delivery fees and ads. And a seller has to cover those costs somewhere. The obvious place is the price tag.
The government even claims Amazon punishes sellers who offer lower prices somewhere else, by burying them in its search results. That claim hasn't been decided in court.

And Prime itself has a price tag in court. In {2025,|twenty twenty-five,} Amazon agreed to pay {$2.5 billion|two and a half billion dollars} to settle claims that it signed people up for Prime without clear consent, and made quitting hard.
So free shipping was never free. The bill is just split up. A little in your Prime fee. A lot in what sellers pay. And some of that, in the prices you see.
Next time a box shows up with free shipping, ask who's on the receipt. Trust me. I'm a price tag.
Free shipping isn't free. It's paid by someone you don't see. Next time: another everyday price, taken apart.
